newsitem.title: USA: Calif. utils must keep stranded costs on books - SEC.
newsitem.headline: Calif. utils must keep stranded costs on books - SEC.

text.p: California's investor-owned utilities will not be able to take stranded costs off balance sheets when they issue securities backed by those assets later this year, according to a recent Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) decision.

Analysts said the decision, issued informally to the utilities, was unlikely to affect credit ratings, but will require some rethinking of the securities and may lead investors to demand higher yields.
"The issues can still be structured in such a way that they can have a high rating," said Mike Sagges with Fitch Investors Service.

The state's three major utilities--Edison International's Southern California Edison Co, PG&E Corp's Pacific Gas & Electric Co and Enova Corp's San Diego Gas & Electric Co--had sought to employ the same accounting practices as issuers of other asset-backed securities.
But the SEC, citing the Financial Accounting Standards Board, ruled the bonds do not meet requirements for a contractual commitment by utility customers to pay them back.
The utility securities will be backed by the expected cash flow from electricity bills, to which special assessments will be added for several years.

Legislation passed in California last year authorized the floating of $10 billion in revenue bonds to help the utilities pay off their "stranded" costs, such as investments in nuclear plants, which were approved by state regulators but are not expected to be cost-competitive as the industry deregulates.
Diane Sable, a spokeswoman for PG&E, said "we don't expect (the SEC decision) to have any impact on structuring of the securities or on our credit rating."
Other states including Pennsylvania, New York and New Jersey are also allowing investor-owned utilties to recoup uneconomic investments through new collaterized debt.
